title: How Phylogenetic Trees Map Relatedness
endLine: Build trees from shared derived states; read relatedness at the nodes.

scenes.tts: Is a trout closer to a shark, or to you? Shark and trout look alike, while you look different. Outward looks can mislead. Phylogenetic trees test which species share a more recent ancestor.
scenes.caption: Is a trout closer to a shark, or to you? Shark and trout look alike, while you look different. Outward looks can mislead. Phylogenetic trees test which species share a more recent ancestor.
scenes.visual: Full-frame branching tree canvas (schematic), filling over 60% of the height. From frame zero, three crisp silhouettes sit along the top tips: shark, trout, and human, with a pulsing question mark spanning shark-trout versus trout-human. Subtle ambient glow travels along faint dashed tree stems underneath; after the opening question settles, a brief title banner fades in and out at the top. As outward looks are mentioned, a temporary bracket around shark and trout dissolves while branching tree paths begin to light up toward a shared ancestor.
scenes.narration: Is a trout closer to a shark, or to you? Shark and trout look alike, while you look different. Outward looks can mislead. Phylogenetic trees test which species share a more recent ancestor.

scenes.tts: To build a tree, compare characters or gene sequences across species. First, add an outgroup, a lineage that branched off earlier. Character states matching it are ancestral, from an older ancestor. Old states cannot show who split last. Only a new, shared derived state marks closest relatives.
scenes.caption: To build a tree, compare characters or gene sequences across species. First, add an outgroup, a lineage that branched off earlier. Character states matching it are ancestral, from an older ancestor. Old states cannot show who split last. Only a new, shared derived state marks closest relatives.
scenes.visual: Same tree canvas (schematic). Small schematic trait icons and striped sequence bars (no molecular structures) slide onto the branches as comparison begins. An outgroup branch extends down-left from the deep root and settles before being named, labelled 'Outgroup'. A teal ancestral tick appears at the root and flows up into every tip, showing it cannot separate shark from trout. Then a bright gold tick appears on the shared branch leading only to trout and human, labelled 'Shared derived', lighting that branch.
scenes.narration: To build a tree, compare characters or gene sequences across species. First, add an outgroup, a lineage that branched off earlier. scenes.tts: Every branching point, or node, marks a common ancestor. Characters change along the branches. Trout is closer to you than to a shark. The ancestor trout shares with you is more recent; it descends from the ancestor shared with the shark.
scenes.caption: Every branching point, or node, marks a common ancestor. Characters change along the branches. Trout is closer to you than to a shark. The ancestor trout shares with you is more recent; it descends from the ancestor shared with the shark.
scenes.visual: Same shark-trout-human tree (schematic), outgroup dimmed. Each branching point glows as a bright node ring before 'node' is spoken; small character-state ticks drift upward along the branches to show change happening on branches. The deeper node joining shark to trout-and-human pulses first, labelled 'Older ancestor'; a bright pulse then travels up the shared branch to the higher node joining trout and human, labelled 'More recent ancestor', highlighting that it descends from the older node.
scenes.narration: Every branching point, or node, marks a common ancestor. Characters change along the branches. Trout is closer to you than to a shark. The ancestor trout shares with you is more recent; it descends from the ancestor shared with the shark.

scenes.tts: Now watch the tree rotate. Suppose we spin the trout and human node so trout sits beside shark. Does spinning that node make trout closer to the shark?
scenes.caption: Now watch the tree rotate. Suppose we spin the trout and human node so trout sits beside shark. Does spinning that node make trout closer to the shark?
scenes.visual: Same tree canvas (schematic). A smooth pivot arrow wraps around the trout-human node; the node swivels halfway around so the trout tip swings left to sit right next to the shark while the human tip swings to the far right, keeping all branch connections intact. A clean high-contrast question card appears above the rotated tree: 'Closer to shark now?'
scenes.narration: Now watch the tree rotate. Suppose we spin the trout and human node so trout sits beside shark. Does spinning that node make trout closer to the shark?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause on the rotated tree (schematic) with 'Closer to shark now?' still on screen. Both ancestor nodes pulse softly in sequence while the tips gently drift so the frame stays alive without giving away the answer.

scenes.tts: No. Rotating a node changes only tip order, never which shared ancestor is more recent. Neither tip order nor the count of nodes between tips shows relatedness. Relatedness lives at the nodes; change lives on the branches. On scaled molecular trees, branch lengths show estimated sequence change, not years.

scenes.visual: Same rotated tree (schematic). The question clears to 'No'; the trout-human node stays highlighted as descending from the deeper shark node while the node smoothly rotates back. Two small extra side twigs sprout on the human branch and fade to show node count between tips does not change the shared ancestor. Next, the branches stretch smoothly into unequal lengths as a schematic molecular phylogram with tick marks representing estimated sequence change, while a crossed-out clock icon marks 'Not years'.

scenes.tts: Trees are hypotheses, and traps can mislead. Two lineages can gain a similar state separately, called convergence. An outgroup can change too. One gene's tree can differ from the species tree. So studies compare several outgroups, use many genes and characters, and report how firmly the data support each node.
scenes.caption: Trees are hypotheses, and traps can mislead. Two lineages can gain a similar state separately, called convergence. An outgroup can change too. scenes.visual: Same tree canvas (schematic). First, two distant branches flash matching amber ticks independently, labelled 'Convergence'. Next, the single outgroup branch shifts colour to show outgroup change, and a thin dashed single-gene tree disagrees with the thicker species tree outline. Then the guards build directly onto the canvas: multiple outgroup branches anchor the root, several parallel sequence strips (no molecular structures) merge into one consensus tree, and support badges light up at each node.
scenes.narration: Trees are hypotheses, and traps can mislead. Two lineages can gain a similar state separately, called convergence. An outgroup can change too. One gene's tree can differ from the species tree. So studies compare several outgroups, use many genes and characters, and report how firmly the data support each node.

scenes.tts: Using trees carries limits too. Turning sequence change into time needs fossils anchored at nodes. In 2012, Parham and colleagues argued a misplaced or misdated fossil carries error into the dates. Related species are not independent points. So phylogenetic regression accounts for shared ancestry when testing traits.

scenes.visual: Same tree canvas (schematic). A schematic fossil pin drops onto an internal node, converting branch lengths onto a time axis; the pin briefly slips off the node and flashes amber as the whole time axis warps, labelled 'Parham and colleagues, 2012', then snaps back. The tree then shifts left beside a small schematic scatter plot whose clustered points link back to one shared branch on the tree; a regression line tilts smoothly as shared ancestry is accounted for, labelled 'Phylogenetic regression'.

scenes.tts: With those guards, trees reshaped biology. In 1977, Woese and George Fox compared short R N A pieces. In 1990, Woese, Otto Kandler and Mark Wheelis proposed three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Many-gene trees now nest eukaryotes inside archaea, closest to a group called Asgard archaea, though the branch is debated.
scenes.caption: With those guards, trees reshaped biology. In 1977, Woese and George Fox compared short RNA pieces. In 1990, Woese, Otto Kandler and Mark Wheelis proposed three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Many-gene trees now nest eukaryotes inside archaea, closest to a group called Asgard archaea, though the branch is debated.
scenes.visual: Same tree canvas zooming out to a deep schematic tree of life. Short striped sequence fragments (no molecular structures) align along the base for '1977', then split smoothly into three bold main trunks labelled 'Bacteria', 'Archaea', and 'Eukarya' with '1990'. Next, the Eukarya branch bends gently inward to nest beside a pulsing 'Asgard archaea' twig inside Archaea, with a soft dashed arc showing the exact branching point remains debated.

scenes.tts: Gene trees broke old rankings of animal bodies. In 1997, Anna Marie Aguinaldo, James Lake and colleagues compared eighteen S ribosomal R N A genes. They grouped nematodes with arthropods and other moulting animals, not annelids.
scenes.caption: Gene trees broke old rankings of animal bodies. In 1997, Anna Marie Aguinaldo, James Lake and colleagues compared 18S ribosomal RNA genes. They grouped nematodes with arthropods and other moulting animals, not annelids.
scenes.visual: Zooming into the animal branch of the same tree canvas (schematic). An old step-like ladder of animal icons breaks apart and reshapes into a branching tree as schematic gene strips sweep across it, tagged '1997'. The nematode branch swings away from the annelid branch and locks onto a shared node with arthropods and other moulting animals, lighting up their shared branch.
scenes.narration: Gene trees broke old rankings of animal bodies. In 1997, Anna Marie Aguinaldo, James Lake and colleagues compared 18S ribosomal RNA genes. They grouped nematodes with arthropods and other moulting animals, not annelids.

scenes.tts: Plant trees shifted too. In 2019, the One Thousand Plant Transcriptomes Initiative compared genes from more than eleven hundred species. Its nuclear gene trees recovered living mosses, liverworts and hornworts as one branch. A living moss is a cousin of vascular plants, not their ancestor. Every tree maps descent from shared nodes, not outward looks.

scenes.visual: Panning across to the land-plant branch of the same tree canvas (schematic). Many fine sequence tracks converge on the tree, tagged '2019'. Living mosses, liverworts, and hornworts gather smoothly onto one shared clade beside the vascular-plant branch, with all living tips aligned evenly at the present to show moss as a cousin, not a root ancestor. The camera pulls slightly back so the glowing nodes and shared derived ticks pulse across the whole carried tree.
